questions.q: How is Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) defined in the provided source?
options: A) An elective surgical procedure to restore sinus rhythm
B) A basic emergency procedure for life support consisting of artificial respiration and manual cardiac massage.
C) The administration of intravenous fluid boluses in hypovolemic shock.
D) Continuous mechanical ventilation in an intensive care setting.
questions.hint: Think about a basic emergency life support procedure combining artificial respiration and manual cardiac compressions.
questions.explanation: CPR is explicitly defined as a basic emergency life support procedure involving artificial respiration and manual cardiac compressions to maintain vital organ perfusion.

questions.q: What is the reported out-of-hospital mortality rate for pediatric cardiac arrest despite the use of CPR?
options: A) Approximately 10%.
B) Approximately 50%.
C) Approximately 90% for infants and children.
D) 100% in all settings.
questions.hint: Out-of-hospital pediatric cardiac arrest carries a mortality rate around 90%.
questions.explanation: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in pediatric populations carries a high mortality rate of approximately 90% for infants and children.

questions.q: According to pediatric resuscitation guidelines, what age and developmental criteria define an infant versus a child?
options: A) Infant: <6 months; Child: 6 months to 10 years.
B) Infant: <1 year of age; Child: 1 year up to 55 kg or presence of pubertal signs.
C) Infant: <2 years; Child: 2 years to 18 years.
D) Infant: <1 month; Child: 1 month to 12 years.
questions.hint: Infant is <1 year; child is 1 year up to 55 kg or signs of puberty.
questions.explanation: Infant guidelines apply to those under 1 year of age, whereas child protocols are utilized from 1 year of age up to 55 kg or until signs of puberty appear (defined as breast development in females and axillary hair in males).

questions.q: What survival rate is associated with rapid bystander CPR in children presenting with respiratory arrest?
options: A) >10% survival rate.
B) >30% survival rate.
C) >70% survival rate.
D) 100% survival rate.
questions.hint: Prompt bystander CPR in primary respiratory arrest yields >70% survival.
questions.explanation: Prompt bystander CPR in children experiencing primary respiratory arrest yields a favorable survival rate of greater than 70%.

questions.q: What is the reported survival rate for pediatric cardiac arrest presenting with Ventricular Fibrillation (VF)?
options: A) 5% survival rate.
B) 30% survival rate.
C) 70% survival rate.
D) 90% survival rate.
questions.hint: Pediatric VF arrest has a reported survival rate of ~30%.
questions.explanation: Pediatric cardiac arrest secondary to ventricular fibrillation carries a survival rate of approximately 30%.

questions.q: What primary sequence of resuscitation actions is recommended to decrease time to initiation of chest compressions?
options: A) A-B-C (Airway, Breathing, Compressions).
B) C-A-B (Compressions, Airway, Breathing).
C) B-A-C (Breathing, Airway, Compressions).
D) C-B-A (Compressions, Breathing, Airway).
questions.hint: Compressions first: C-A-B.
questions.explanation: Resuscitation guidelines advocate the C-A-B sequence over A-B-C to reduce the 'no blood flow' time by initiating chest compressions immediately.

questions.q: By approximately how many seconds is the first ventilation delayed when using the C-A-B sequence instead of A-B-C?
options: A) 2 seconds.
B) 6 seconds.
C) 30 seconds.
D) 60 seconds.
questions.hint: Starting with C-A-B delays the first breath by only about 6 seconds.
questions.explanation: Transitioning from A-B-C to C-A-B delays the delivery of the first ventilation by only approximately 6 seconds while ensuring rapid blood flow delivery.

questions.q: What are the primary aims of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation?
options: A) To administer high-dose steroids and induce deep sedation.
B) To provide oxygen to vital organs (heart, brain, lung) until normal circulation is restored, establish an airway, initiate breathing, and maintain proper circulation.
C) To replace circulating volume with colloid fluids.
D) To evaluate long-term cognitive development.
questions.hint: Oxygenate vital organs (heart, brain, lungs), establish airway, start breathing, and support circulation.
questions.explanation: The fundamental objectives of CPR are oxygen delivery to the heart, brain, and lungs, airway establishment, breathing initiation, and circulation maintenance.

questions.q: Which non-traumatic environmental or medical conditions are listed as causes of pediatric cardiopulmonary arrest?
options: A) Allergic reactions, asphyxia, choking, drowning, drug reactions/overdoses, and electric shock.
B) Isolated hypercalcemia and mild viral colds.
C) Congenital cataracts and hypertrophic skin lesions.
D) Essential hypertension and mild asthma.
questions.hint: Think of allergic reactions, asphyxia, choking, drowning, drug overdoses, and electric shock.
questions.explanation: Common triggers for pediatric arrest include severe allergic reactions, asphyxiation, foreign body choking, submersion drowning, toxic drug overdoses, and electrical injury.

questions.q: What clinical signs confirm the presence of cardiac arrest at the patient's bedside?
options: A) Absence of movement, absence of breathing, no response to rescue breaths, no pulse, or an arrest rhythm on a monitor.
B) Isolated fever with a bounding pulse.
C) Tachypnea with normal capillary refill.
D) Hypertension and decorticate posturing.
questions.hint: No movement, no normal breathing, no pulse, or an arrest rhythm on the monitor.
questions.explanation: Cardiac arrest is diagnosed clinically by unresponsiveness, lack of spontaneous respiration/gasping, absence of palpable central pulse within 10 seconds, or visible arrest rhythms on ECG.

questions.q: What is the recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio for SINGLE-RESCUER pediatric CPR?
questions.hint: A single rescuer uses 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
questions.explanation: For a single rescuer performing CPR on an infant or child, the standard compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

questions.q: What is the recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio for TWO OR MORE RESCUERS performing pediatric CPR?
questions.hint: Two or more rescuers use 15 compressions to 2 breaths in pediatrics.
questions.explanation: When two or more healthcare providers or trained rescuers are present, the pediatric compression-to-ventilation ratio changes to 15 compressions to 2 breaths.

questions.q: What is the target chest compression rate for pediatric CPR across all age groups?
options: A) 60 to 80 compressions per minute.
B) 80 to 100 compressions per minute.
C) 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
D) 140 to 160 compressions per minute.
questions.hint: Target 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
questions.explanation: Chest compressions in infants, children, and adolescents must be delivered at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.

questions.q: What is the maximum allowable time for assessing both breathing and pulse simultaneously before starting compressions?
options: A) 5 seconds.
B) No more than 10 seconds.
C) 30 seconds.
D) 60 seconds.
questions.hint: Take no longer than 10 seconds to check breathing and pulse.
questions.explanation: Pulse and breathing assessment must occur simultaneously and take no longer than 10 seconds to avoid delaying chest compressions.

questions.q: If a pediatric victim has a palpable pulse BUT is not breathing normally (respiratory arrest), what is the correct rescue breathing rate?
options: A) 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds (10 to 12 breaths/min).
B) 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds (20 to 30 breaths/min).
C) 1 breath every 10 seconds (6 breaths/min).
D) 10 breaths every 5 seconds.
questions.hint: Deliver 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds (20–30 breaths/min) for rescue breathing with a pulse.
questions.explanation: Updated CPR guidelines mandate delivering 1 rescue breath every 2 to 3 seconds (20 to 30 breaths/min) for infants and children with a pulse who require ventilatory support.

questions.q: In a non-breathing infant or child with a pulse, at what heart rate threshold with poor perfusion must chest compressions be added to rescue breathing?
options: A) Pulse ≤100 beats/min.
B) Pulse ≤60 beats/min with signs of poor perfusion.
C) Pulse ≤40 beats/min.
D) Compressions are added only when pulse is 0.
questions.hint: Start compressions if heart rate is ≤60/min with signs of poor perfusion.
questions.explanation: If an infant or child has a heart rate of 60 beats/min or less with evidence of poor systemic perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation, chest compressions must be initiated immediately.

questions.q: Where should a rescuer palpate for a central pulse in an INFANT (<1 year of age)?
options: A) Carotid artery.
B) Brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm midway between elbow and shoulder.
C) Radial artery at the wrist.
D) Popliteal artery behind the knee.
questions.hint: Check the brachial artery on the inner upper arm in infants.
questions.explanation: In infants (<1 year), the central pulse is assessed at the brachial artery using 2–3 fingers placed on the inner upper arm.

questions.q: Where should a rescuer assess for a pulse in a CHILD (1 year to puberty)?
options: A) Brachial artery only.
B) Carotid or Femoral pulse.
C) Radial pulse only.
D) Temporal artery.
questions.hint: Check the carotid or femoral artery in children.
questions.explanation: In children over 1 year of age, the rescuer assesses the carotid artery in the neck groove or the femoral artery in the inner groin.

questions.q: What anatomical landmark is used to locate the Femoral Pulse during pediatric resuscitation?
options: A) Radial styloid process.
B) 2–3 fingers in the inner thigh between the hip bone and pubic bone.
C) Upper margin of the clavicle.
D) Lateral malleolus.
questions.hint: 2–3 fingers in the inner thigh between the hip bone and pubic bone.
questions.explanation: The femoral pulse is located by placing 2–3 fingers in the anterior inner thigh, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine (hip) and pubic symphysis.

questions.q: What key step must be performed FIRST before assessing unresponsiveness or initiating CPR?
options: A) Connect an electrocardiogram monitor.
B) Verify scene safety.
C) Administer IV epinephrine.
D) Perform endotracheal intubation.
questions.hint: Always make sure the scene is safe first.
questions.explanation: The absolute first step in any resuscitation attempt is verifying that the environment is safe for both rescuers and the victim.

questions.q: What is the recommended chest compression depth for INFANTS (<1 year of age)?
options: A) 2 cm (0.75 inches).
B) At least one-third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches).
C) 6 cm (2.4 inches).
D) 1 cm (0.5 inches).
questions.hint: At least 1/3 AP chest diameter, about 4 cm (1.5 inches) in infants.
questions.explanation: In infants, compressions must depress the sternum at least one-third the anteroposterior chest diameter, corresponding to approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches).

questions.q: What is the recommended chest compression depth for CHILDREN (1 year to puberty)?
options: A) 2 cm (0.75 inches).
B) At least one-third the AP diameter of the chest, approximately 5 cm (2 inches).
C) 8 cm (3.2 inches).
D) 1 cm (0.5 inches).
questions.hint: At least 1/3 AP chest diameter, about 5 cm (2 inches) in children.
questions.explanation: In children, compression depth should be one-third the AP diameter of the chest, or approximately 5 cm (2 inches).

questions.q: What is the recommended chest compression depth for ADOLESCENTS during CPR?
options: A) 3 cm (1.2 inches).
B) At least 5 cm (2 inches) but not greater than 6 cm (2.4 inches).
C) 7 to 9 cm.
D) 2 cm maximum.
questions.hint: At least 5 cm (2 inches) and no more than 6 cm (2.4 inches) in adolescents.
questions.explanation: For adolescents, chest compressions should reach a depth of at least 5 cm (2 inches) while avoiding excessive depths greater than 6 cm (2.4 inches).

questions.q: Which manual technique is recommended for single-rescuer chest compressions in an INFANT?
options: A) Two-thumb encircling-hands technique.
B) Two-finger technique (using index and middle fingers placed on the lower half of the sternum).
C) Two-hand interlocked technique.
D) Palm heel compression on the abdomen.
questions.hint: Single rescuer on an infant uses two fingers on the lower half of the sternum.
questions.explanation: Single rescuers compress an infant's chest using the two-finger technique placed on the lower half of the sternum.

questions.q: Which compression technique is preferred for NEWBORNS or when TWO RESCUERS are performing infant CPR?
options: A) Two-finger technique.
B) Two-thumb encircling-hands technique.
C) One-hand palm technique.
D) Back blows only.
questions.hint: Two-thumb encircling-hands technique for newborns and two-rescuer infant CPR.
questions.explanation: The two-thumb encircling-hands technique is recommended for newborns and two-rescuer infant CPR because it generates superior coronary perfusion pressure.

questions.q: What compression hand techniques are used for a YOUNG CHILD versus an OLDER CHILD/ADOLESCENT?
options: A) Young child: Two fingers; Older child: Two thumbs.
B) Young child: One-hand technique (heel of one hand); Older child: Two-hands technique (interlocked hands).
C) Young child: Two hands; Older child: One finger.
D) Both receive two-thumb encircling compressions.
questions.hint: One hand for a small young child; two interlocked hands for an older child/adolescent.
questions.explanation: Rescuers may use a one-hand technique (heel of one hand) for small young children, and a two-hand interlocked technique for older children and adolescents.

questions.q: Where precisely on the anatomical chest wall must chest compressions be delivered?
options: A) Over the xiphoid process.
B) Over the lower half of the sternum.
C) Over the upper third of the sternum.
D) Over the left rib cage directly above the apex.
questions.hint: Lower half of the sternum, avoiding the xiphoid.
questions.explanation: Compressions must be performed over the lower half of the sternum, avoiding the xiphoid tip.

questions.q: Why must compressions directly over the Xiphoid Process be strictly avoided?
options: A) It prevents adequate chest recoil.
B) Compression of the xiphoid process can cause mechanical trauma to underlying internal organs like the liver, spleen, or stomach.
C) It causes immediate ventricular fibrillation.
D) It reduces artificial tidal volume.
questions.hint: Compressing the xiphoid can injure underlying organs such as the liver, spleen, or stomach.
questions.explanation: Compressing the xiphoid process risks fracturing the tip and lacerating underlying abdominal viscera such as the liver, spleen, or stomach.

questions.q: Why is allowing FULL CHEST RECOIL between compressions a critical quality component of CPR?
options: A) It allows time for rescue breaths to be delivered.
B) It permits complete cardiac refill during diastole, optimizing coronary and systemic perfusion pressure.
C) It reduces rib fracture incidence.
D) It prevents gastric inflation.
questions.hint: Full recoil lets the heart refill with blood during diastole.
questions.explanation: Allowing the chest wall to fully recoil after each compression enables venous return and ventricular refill during diastole, preserving cardiac output.

questions.q: What are the four core pillars defining HIGH-QUALITY CPR according to international guidelines?
options: A) 1. Adequate compression rate (100–120/min) and depth, 2. Minimizing interruptions in compressions, 3. Allowing full chest recoil, and 4. Avoiding excessive ventilation.
B) 1. Continuous IV fluids, 2. High-dose epinephrine, 3. Immediate intubation, and 4. Ice baths.
C) 1. Rapid transport, 2. Atropine push, 3. Abdominal thrusts, and 4. Hyperventilation.
D) 1. Preload elevation, 2. SVR expansion, 3. Defibrillation for all, and 4. Oxygen restriction.
questions.hint: Rate/depth, minimal pauses, full chest recoil, and no excessive ventilation.
questions.explanation: High-quality CPR demands correct rate/depth, complete chest recoil, minimal pauses, and avoiding hyperventilation.

questions.q: Which four cardiac arrest rhythms are recognized, and how are they categorized?
options: A) Asystole & PEA (Non-shockable); VF & Pulseless VT (Shockable).
B) Sinus Bradycardia & SVT (Shockable); Asystole & AF (Non-shockable).
C) Atrial Fibrillation & Flutter (Non-shockable); Ventricular ectopics (Shockable).
D) All 4 rhythms are shockable.
questions.hint: Asystole and PEA are non-shockable; VF and pulseless VT are shockable.
questions.explanation: Cardiac arrest rhythms are divided into Non-shockable (Asystole and Pulseless Electrical Activity) and Shockable (Ventricular Fibrillation and Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia).

questions.q: For NON-SHOCKABLE rhythms (Asystole and PEA), what is the drug of choice, route, dose, and administration frequency?
options: A) Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO given as soon as possible, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes.
B) Amiodarone 10 mg/kg IV push given once.
C) Atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV given every 2 minutes.
D) Epinephrine 1 mg/kg IV push given every 10 minutes.
questions.hint: Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO ASAP, then every 3–5 minutes.
questions.explanation: In non-shockable rhythms, Epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg IV/IO) should be administered as early as possible after arrest recognition and repeated every 3 to 5 minutes during ongoing CPR.

questions.q: What are the recommended initial and subsequent manual Defibrillation energy doses for shockable rhythms (VF/pVT)?
options: A) Initial: 10 J/kg; Subsequent: 20 J/kg.
B) Initial: 2 Joules/kg; Subsequent: 4 Joules/kg (up to maximum 10 J/kg).
C) Initial: 50 Joules fixed for all ages.
D) Initial: 0.5 J/kg; Subsequent: 1 J/kg.
questions.hint: Start at 2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg, up to a max of 10 J/kg.
questions.explanation: Manual defibrillation energy setting is 2 J/kg for the first shock, increasing to 4 J/kg for subsequent shocks, with a maximum ceiling of 10 J/kg.

questions.q: During resuscitation for SHOCKABLE rhythms (VF/pVT), when is Epinephrine administered according to algorithmic timing?
options: A) Before delivering the first shock.
B) After the 3rd shock (if VF/pVT persists) and then every alternate shock cycle (every 3–5 minutes).
C) Epinephrine is contraindicated in shockable rhythms.
D) Continuous IV infusion at 1 mg/kg/min.
questions.hint: In shockable rhythms, give epinephrine after the 3rd shock and every 3–5 minutes thereafter.
questions.explanation: In refractory VF/pVT, epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg IV/IO) is administered after the 3rd shock and repeated every 3–5 minutes.

questions.q: What antiarrhythmic agent is indicated for refractory VF/pVT, and what is its dosage and timing?
options: A) Lidocaine 50 mg/kg single bolus.
B) Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV/IO bolus given after the 3rd shock, which may be repeated up to 2 times (total 3 doses) for refractory VF/pVT.
C) Procainamide 15 mg/kg IV over 1 hour.
D) Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg rapid push.
questions.hint: Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV/IO after the 3rd shock for refractory VF/pVT.
questions.explanation: Amiodarone (5 mg/kg IV/IO) is indicated for shock-refractory VF/pVT after the 3rd and 5th shocks.

questions.q: If Amiodarone is unavailable during resuscitation for refractory VF/pVT, what alternative antiarrhythmic regimen can be administered?
options: A) High-dose Calcium Gluconate IV.
B) Lidocaine at a loading dose of 1 mg/kg IV, followed by a maintenance infusion of 20 to 50 mcg/kg/minute.
C) Sodium Bicarbonate 10 mEq/kg.
D) Esmolol infusion 500 mcg/kg.
questions.hint: Lidocaine 1 mg/kg IV loading bolus, then 20–50 mcg/kg/min infusion.
questions.explanation: Lidocaine serves as the alternative antiarrhythmic, dosed at 1 mg/kg IV loading bolus followed by a 20–50 mcg/kg/min infusion.

questions.q: What is the recommendation regarding the use of Atropine and Pacing in pediatric Asystole?
options: A) Atropine is mandatory every 2 minutes.
B) Atropine and transcutaneous pacing are NOT used/recommended for Asystole.
C) Pacing is the first-line treatment for Asystole.
D) High-dose atropine replaces epinephrine.
questions.hint: Neither atropine nor pacing is recommended for pediatric asystole.
questions.explanation: Current resuscitation guidelines state that routine atropine and cardiac pacing are not used for pediatric asystole.

questions.q: What proportion of pediatric cardiac arrests present with Shockable Rhythms (VF/pVT)?
questions.hint: About 15–20% of pediatric arrests present with shockable rhythms.
questions.explanation: Shockable rhythms (VF and pulseless VT) account for approximately 15% to 20% of initial pediatric cardiac arrest presentations.

questions.q: What is the recommendation regarding Automated External Defibrillator (AED) usage in children up to 8 years of age?
options: A) AEDs are strictly prohibited in children under 8 years.
B) An AED equipped with pediatric cables/attenuator (delivering a maximum biphasic shock of 50 Joules) is preferred, but a standard adult AED may be used if a pediatric attenuator is unavailable.
C) Adult AEDs must never be attached under any circumstances.
D) AEDs must deliver a minimum of 200 Joules to children.
questions.hint: Pediatric attenuator (~50 J) is preferred under 8 years, though a standard AED can be used if unavailable.
questions.explanation: Pediatric attenuator cables (limiting dose to ~50 J) are preferred up to 8 years of age, though standard AEDs can be used if pediatric cables are absent.

questions.q: Immediately after delivering a manual shock or AED shock, what action must rescuers perform?
options: A) Pause compressions for 2 minutes to evaluate the radial pulse.
B) Resume high-quality CPR immediately (starting with chest compressions) for 2 minutes before re-checking rhythm or pulse.
C) Deliver a second shock immediately.
D) Administer IV bolus of normal saline.
questions.hint: Resume chest compressions right away for 2 minutes after a shock.
questions.explanation: Rescuers must resume chest compressions immediately after shock delivery without delaying for pulse checks, completing a 2-minute cycle of CPR first.

questions.q: What reversible etiologies must be systematically evaluated and treated during cardiac arrest resuscitation, summarized as the '4 Hs and 4 Ts'?
options: A) 4 Hs: Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia; 4 Ts: Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxic substances, Thromboembolic phenomena.
B) 4 Hs: Hypertension, Hyperglycemia, Hepatitis, Hydrocephalus; 4 Ts: Trauma, Tumor, Tuberculosis, Typhoid.
C) 4 Hs: Hyponatremia, Hypocalcemia, Heparin, Herpes; 4 Ts: Tetany, Tetanus, Trachoma, Tonsillitis.
D) 4 Hs: Heart failure, Headache, Hemorrhage, Hemolysis; 4 Ts: Tachycardia, Tachypnea, Thrombosis, Toxicity.
questions.hint: Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thromboembolism.
questions.explanation: Reversible causes of arrest are grouped into 4 Hs (Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia) and 4 Ts (Tension pneumothorax, Cardiac tamponade, Toxins, Thromboembolism).

questions.q: Why are infants and young children particularly susceptible to rapid hypothermia during resuscitation attempts?
options: A) They have excessive subcutaneous brown fat.
B) They have a large surface area relative to body mass and minimal subcutaneous adipose tissue.
C) Their metabolic rate is zero during resuscitation.
D) They lack sweat glands.
questions.hint: High body surface area-to-mass ratio and thin subcutaneous fat.
questions.explanation: High body surface area-to-mass ratio and thin subcutaneous insulation cause rapid body heat loss in pediatric patients.

questions.q: What physiological effect does severe Hypothermia (core temperature < 35°C) have on the resuscitation process?
options: A) It improves cardiac contractility.
B) It makes resuscitation significantly more difficult by increasing metabolic demands, worsening acidosis, and impairing drug metabolism.
C) It eliminates the risk of dysrhythmias.
D) It automatically restores spontaneous circulation.
questions.hint: Hypothermia (<35°C) complicates resuscitation, worsens acidosis, and alters metabolism.
questions.explanation: Core hypothermia (<35°C) refractory to environmental warming impairs cardiac responsiveness, exacerbates acidosis, and complicates resuscitation.

questions.q: In post-cardiac arrest care following Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC), what interventions are indicated for comatose children?
options: A) Immediate discharge home.
B) Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) and continuous electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring.
C) High-dose corticosteroids and forced hyperventilation.
D) Induction of severe hyperthermia.
questions.hint: Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) and continuous EEG monitoring.
questions.explanation: Post-ROSC care for non-alert children includes targeted temperature regulation (preventing fever/maintaining normothermia) and continuous EEG monitoring to detect subclinical seizures.

questions.q: What physiological parameters must be strictly controlled during post-cardiac arrest management to prevent secondary brain injury?
options: A) Prevention and treatment of Hypotension, Hyperoxia or Hypoxia, and Hypercapnia or Hypocapnia.
B) Maintenance of blood pressure below 50 mmHg.
C) Target SpO2 of 100% using hyperbaric oxygen.
D) Inducing hypercapnia to increase cerebral flow.
questions.hint: Avoid hypotension, hypoxia/hyperoxia, and hypocapnia/hypercapnia.
questions.explanation: Neuroprotective post-arrest care requires strict arterial blood gas and blood pressure control to avoid ischemia or reperfusion injury from hypoxia, hyperoxia, hypotension, or hypocapnia/hypercapnia.

questions.q: What ventilation strategy should be used once an Advanced Airway (endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway) is placed during CPR?
options: A) Pause compressions for 2 seconds every 15 compressions to deliver 2 breaths.
B) Deliver 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds (20 to 30 breaths/minute) continuously WITHOUT pausing chest compressions.
C) Deliver 50 breaths per minute with hyperventilation.
D) Stop ventilations completely.
questions.hint: Continuous compressions with 1 breath every 2–3 seconds (20–30/min).
questions.explanation: With an advanced airway in place, chest compressions are given continuously at 100–120/min without pauses, while 1 ventilation is delivered every 2–3 seconds (20–30 breaths/min).

questions.q: Which mechanical traumatic complications can occur as a direct result of chest compressions during CPR?
options: A) Rib and sternal fractures, pneumothorax, pericardial tamponade, pulmonary contusion, aspiration, and aortic laceration.
B) Isolated retinal detachment.
C) Intracranial calcifications.
D) Femoral artery thrombosis.
questions.hint: Rib/sternal fractures, pneumothorax, tamponade, pulmonary contusion, aspiration, aortic injury.
questions.explanation: Complications of high-quality CPR include thoracic skeletal trauma (rib/sternal fractures), pleural/cardiac injury (pneumothorax, tamponade, contusion, aortic laceration), and gastric contents aspiration.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the timing of initial Epinephrine administration and survival in non-shockable pediatric cardiac arrest?
options: A) Delayed administration improves survival.
B) The earlier epinephrine is administered after CPR initiation, the higher the likelihood of ROSC and intact survival.
C) Timing has no impact on survival.
D) Epinephrine should only be given after 20 minutes of CPR.
questions.hint: Earlier epinephrine in non-shockable arrest is linked to higher ROSC and survival.
questions.explanation: Clinical trial data demonstrate that early administration of epinephrine in non-shockable rhythms directly correlates with increased ROSC and survival rates.

questions.q: What are the components of the Pediatric Chain of Survival?
options: A) Prevention and preparedness, Activation of emergency response system, High-quality CPR (including early defibrillation), Advanced resuscitation interventions, Post-cardiac arrest care, and Recovery.
B) Intubation, Antibiotics, Surgery, Rehabilitation.
C) Triage, Isolation, Dialysis, Transfer.
D) Oxygenation, Cooling, Steroids, Discharge.
questions.hint: Prevention/preparedness, EMS activation, high-quality CPR/defibrillation, advanced care, post-arrest care, recovery.
questions.explanation: The AHA Chain of Survival comprises 6 linked steps: Prevention/preparedness, EMS activation, high-quality CPR/defibrillation, advanced life support, post-arrest care, and long-term recovery.

questions.q: A 9-month-old infant (weight 8 kg) is brought to the emergency department in collapse. Assessment shows no spontaneous breathing and a brachial pulse of 40 beats/min with cold cyanotic extremities. Two healthcare providers are present. What initial BLS action and ratio are needed, what compression technique/rate/depth apply, and what is the priority drug protocol for Asystole?
options: A) Give rescue breaths only at 10 breaths/min; No compressions; Epinephrine 1 mg IV once.

B) 1. Initiate immediate CPR (compressions + ventilation) due to HR <60/min with poor perfusion; Ratio = 15:2 (two rescuers). 2. Technique = Two-thumb encircling-hands technique; Rate = 100–120/min; Depth = 1/3 AP diameter (~4 cm). 3. Rhythm = Asystole (Non-shockable); Administer Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.08 mg) immediately and repeat every 3 to 5 minutes during ongoing 2-minute CPR cycles.
C) Perform 30:2 CPR using 1 hand to depth of 6 cm; Defibrillate at 50 Joules.
D) Give atropine 0.5 mg IV and place transcutaneous pacing pads.
questions.hint: HR <60 with poor perfusion + 2 rescuers = 15:2 two-thumb encircling CPR (100–120/min, ~4 cm); Asystole gets Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (0.08 mg) IV/IO q3–5min.
questions.explanation: 1) Bradycardia <60 bpm with poor perfusion requires immediate CPR; two rescuers use a 15:2 ratio. 2) Two-rescuer infant compressions use the two-thumb encircling-hands technique at 100–120/min to ~4 cm (1/3 AP diameter). 3) Asystole is non-shockable, so give Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.08 mg for 8 kg) immediately and repeat every 3–5 minutes.
